title: Odile and the Sigil
premise: Quentin Zhou has spent nine years keeping the ledgers of the Vesper Guild, which trades in impossible things through a gate that must never open twice. When the old gods resume answering prayers, the gate begins to hum, and Quentin discovers her own name written in a ledger older than the guild itself. The god answering the kingdom's prayers is not a god at all but the sigil wearing the king's crown, and its bargains are eating the memories of everyone who prays. To unbind the king, Quentin must trade the one memory the sigil cannot price — the night she survived, which cost her sister — and in doing so she learns the gate was built to hold her, not the gods. The book ends with the king freed, the guild dissolved, and Quentin walking out of the ledger-house with her sister's face remembered at last, into a winter that is only weather now.
about_author: Petra Yarrow is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing guild records in a coastal trading city before turning to fiction. She writes fantasies about paperwork, bargains, and the people who keep both.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Impossible Things
chapters.summary: Quentin Zhou audits the Vesper Guild's winter accounts, noting a prayer-transaction she never recorded. Her POV establishes her meticulous, guarded voice and the guild's rules. The beat: quiet unease — a number that shouldn't exist has appeared in her own handwriting.

chapters.title: Prayers, Answered
chapters.summary: Word spreads through the city that prayers are being answered for the first time in a century. Quentin interviews a fishwife whose dead husband returned for one evening — at the cost of her memory of him. Quentin's POV; the beat is dread disguised as professional curiosity.

chapters.title: The Hum in the Gate
chapters.summary: Quentin inspects the sealed gate beneath the guild-house and hears it humming her name. Guildmaster Oren Vesper dismisses her concerns and burns her report. Her POV; the emotional beat is the first crack in her loyalty to the institution that saved her.

chapters.title: A King Who Forgets His Own Edicts
chapters.summary: Summoned to the palace to reconcile the crown's accounts, Quentin watches King Aldric sign an edict he wrote that morning and not recognize it. Courtier POV briefly, then Quentin's. The beat: horror — she recognizes the same forgetting in the king that she saw in the fishwife.

chapters.title: The Thing Wearing the Crown
chapters.summary: Quentin follows the king's shadow into the throne room at night and sees the sigil — a god-shaped absence seated inside Aldric, granting wishes and consuming the wisher's past. Her POV; the beat is terror and a terrible recognition, as if she's met it before.

chapters.title: What the Old Ledgers Say
chapters.summary: Quentin breaks into the guild's forbidden archive and finds a ledger older than the guild, in which her own name is the final entry of a nine-year-old bargain. Oren catches her. Her POV; the beat is betrayal — the guild didn't shelter her, it purchased her.

chapters.title: Nine Years Ago
chapters.summary: A flashback chapter in Quentin's POV: the plague winter, her sister Wren's death, the stranger from the guild who offered survival in exchange for the memory of the night it happened. The beat is grief finally given its shape, and the reader learns what Quentin traded.

chapters.title: Running the Accounts
chapters.summary: Quentin flees the guild-house and takes refuge with Sable, a disgraced priestess of the old gods who has been tracking answered prayers across the city. Sable's POV; the beat is reluctant alliance — two women who both kept books for powers they mistrusted.

chapters.title: The Price List
chapters.summary: Sable shows Quentin the pattern: every answered prayer costs a memory, and the sigil is hoarding them to finish unbinding itself from the king. Quentin's POV; the beat is cold clarity — she understands the arithmetic of the thing now, and arithmetic is her weapon.

chapters.title: The Guild Closes Its Doors
chapters.summary: Oren Vesper declares the guild neutral and seals the gate with Quentin's ledger-entry as the lock, meaning she can never leave the city or die free. Her POV; the beat is claustrophobic rage — the cage was always the paperwork.

chapters.title: Breaking into the Palace
chapters.summary: Quentin and Sable infiltrate the winter court disguised as accountants for the crown's debts. Quentin's POV; the beat is tense competence — she is best when forging, and for the first time she forges for herself.

chapters.title: The Man Inside the King
chapters.summary: Quentin reaches Aldric privately and finds a flicker of the real king, who begs her, in a child's voice, to make it stop. His POV for the first time; the beat is heartbreak — the god's host is still alive in there, and he remembers nothing but fear.

chapters.title: The Sigil Speaks
chapters.summary: The sigil notices Quentin and offers her anything, including Wren's memory returned intact, if she walks away. Her POV; the beat is temptation rendered as bookkeeping — it shows her the exact ledger line where her sister lives.

chapters.title: What Quentin Refuses
chapters.summary: Quentin refuses the bargain and the sigil takes Sable's memories of her order as punishment, leaving the priestess unable to remember why she fights. Sable's POV; the beat is guilt — Quentin's war is now costing other people their pasts.

chapters.title: The Unbinding Rite
chapters.summary: Sable, half-erased, reconstructs the old rite from fragments: the sigil can only be unbound by someone who owes it a debt and pays it in full, willingly. Quentin's POV; the beat is grim resolve — she is the only debtor alive whose debt is a memory.

chapters.title: Storming the Ledger-House
chapters.summary: Quentin returns to the guild to steal back her original contract, fighting through Oren's wardens. Oren's POV in the second half, revealing he made the same trade decades ago and has nothing left inside. The beat is pity for her enemy.

chapters.title: The Original Entry
chapters.summary: Quentin reads the full contract: the guild didn't buy her memory — the sigil did, nine years ago, planting her at the gate as a future key. Her POV; the beat is vertigo — her whole survival was a down payment on this winter.

chapters.title: The Long Winter Falls
chapters.summary: The sigil, nearly free of the king, stops granting wishes and begins taking memories without consent; the city starts forgetting itself street by street. Multiple brief POVs; the beat is escalating apocalypse rendered as mass amnesia.

chapters.title: The Throne Room, Again
chapters.summary: Quentin confronts the sigil on the eve of its freedom and offers to pay her debt: the night of Wren's death, in full, willingly — but she has rewritten the terms, binding the payment to the rite itself. Her POV; the beat is the climax's first movement, a gambler's calm.

chapters.title: What the Sigil Cannot Price
chapters.summary: The sigil takes the memory — and discovers Quentin's memory of Wren was never grief alone but the proof that love outlasts erasure, a thing it cannot hold. The unbinding rite ignites through it. Quentin's POV; the beat is sacrificial triumph as the sigil unravels.

chapters.title: The King, Unbound
chapters.summary: Aldric wakes in his own body with his past returned, while the sigil's hoarded memories rain back over the city. Quentin, emptied of Wren, sits in the snow. Aldric's POV; the beat is exhausted grace — survival's price paid, and the question of what remains.

chapters.title: Spring Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Quentin closes the guild's final ledger, dissolves the Vesper Guild, and walks out of the ledger-house — where a young woman with Wren's laugh asks her the way to the market. Quentin's POV; the final beat: memory returns not as it was, but as something she can carry.
